title: "Breaking the chain in a self-exciting point process: estimating the repeat crimes an arrest prevents"
author: "Andrew P. Wheeler"
abstract: |
  Self-exciting point process models of crime let each crime temporarily
  raise the rate of further crimes nearby, but they have no way for the
  police to end a chain. I add a term that does. When a crime has an
  arrest, the triggering it had left is multiplied by a factor kappa, where
  zero is an arrest that ends the chain and one is no effect. The arrest
  enters at the time it happens, so a fast arrest removes more than a slow
  one, and the model avoids the bias of treating an eventual arrest as a
  fixed trait of the crime. The fitted model gives the number of follow-on
  crimes each arrest prevented and the total. In simulations it recovers
  kappa and the count of crimes prevented, including when crimes come from
  offender sprees that arrests cut short, while the fixed-trait version
  misses from two fifths to nearly all of the crimes prevented. I apply it
  in two cities that publish arrest times linked to crime reports. Of
  66,355 car prowls (thefts from motor vehicles) in Seattle, Washington,
  2019 to mid-2026, 7% were triggered by an earlier car prowl, half of those
  within four hours and nearly all within a block or two. An arrest cuts
  the remaining triggering by 95% (kappa 0.05, 95% interval 0.00 to 0.24).
  The 722 arrests prevented an estimated 42 car prowls (95% interval 26 to
  56). The effect on a chain is large, but chains are short and arrests are
  rare, so the total is small. For 27,385 shooting incidents in Chicago,
  Illinois, 2016 to mid-2026, whose linked arrests match published arrest

  hour), and the arrest effect cannot be distinguished from no effect

```{python}
#| label: setup
import json
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Markdown

from arresthawkes import model, plots

plots.use_theme()
R = Path("results")
num = lambda v, d=0: f"{v:,.{d}f}"
pct = lambda v, d=0: f"{v * 100:.{d}f}%"
pval = lambda p: "< 0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"{p:.3f}"
def show(df, left=1):
    """Markdown table; cells are kept as written (no number re-parsing), the
    first `left` columns left-aligned and the rest right-aligned."""
    align = ["left"] * left + ["right"] * (df.shape[1] - left)
    return Markdown(df.astype(str).to_markdown(index=False, disable_numparse=True, colalign=align))
CRIMES = ["shootings", "carprowl"]
CNAME = {"shootings": "Shootings (Chicago)", "carprowl": "Car prowls (Seattle)"}

# --- Simulation -------------------------------------------------------------
# "null" is a scenario name here, not a missing value
sim = pd.concat([pd.read_csv(f, keep_default_na=False, na_values=[""])
                 for f in sorted((R / "sim" / "rows").glob("*.csv"))], ignore_index=True)
SCEN = {"model": "Model", "null": "No arrest effect", "late": "Late arrests", "confounded": "Confounded",
        "spree": "Sprees", "spree_clear": "Sprees, earlier crimes cleared"}
KTRUE = {"model": 0.3, "null": 1.0, "late": 0.3, "confounded": 0.3, "spree": 0.0, "spree_clear": 0.0}
METH = {"dynamic": "Arrest at its time", "static": "Arrest as fixed mark",
        "dynamic + covariate": "Arrest at its time + covariate"}
sim["ktrue"] = sim["scenario"].map(KTRUE)
sim["kappa"] = np.exp(sim["log_kappa"])
sim["cover_k"] = (sim["kappa_low"] <= sim["ktrue"] * 1.0000001) & (sim["ktrue"] <= sim["kappa_high"])
# with a true kappa of zero the interval covers when it runs to the bottom of the grid
sim.loc[sim["ktrue"] == 0, "cover_k"] = sim["kappa_low"] <= np.exp(-7) * 1.0001
_pl, _ph = model.prediction_interval(sim["est"], sim["low"], sim["high"], sim["direct"], sim["n0"])
sim["cover"] = (_pl <= sim["truth"]) & (sim["truth"] <= _ph)
sim["err"] = sim["est"] - sim["truth"]


def sim_summary(g):
    dyn = g["kappa_low"].notna().all()
    return pd.Series({
        "reps": len(g), "n": g["n"].mean(), "arrests": g["arrests"].mean(), "ktrue": g["ktrue"].iloc[0],
        "kmed": g["kappa"].median(), "cover_k": g["cover_k"].mean() if dyn else np.nan,
        "reject": (g["lr_p"] < 0.05).mean(), "truth": g["truth"].mean(), "est": g["est"].mean(),
        "rmse": np.sqrt((g["err"] ** 2).mean()), "cover": g["cover"].mean() if dyn else np.nan,
        "theta": g["theta"].mean(), "omega": g["omega"].mean(), "sigma": g["sigma"].mean(),
    })


simsum = sim.groupby(["scenario", "method"]).apply(sim_summary, include_groups=False)
SS = lambda scen, meth, col: simsum.loc[(scen, meth), col]
n_rep = int(sim.groupby("scenario")["seed"].nunique().min())

# --- Chicago shootings and Seattle car prowls ------------------------------
_cm = json.load(open("data/chicago_meta.json"))
meta = {"shootings": _cm["chicago_shootings"], "shootings_violent": _cm["chicago_shootings_violent"],
        "carprowl": json.load(open("data/seattle_meta.json"))["carprowl"]}
S = {c: json.load(open(R / "models" / f"{c}_summary.json")) for c in CRIMES}
tab = lambda c, name: pd.read_csv(R / "models" / f"{c}_{name}.csv")
ci = lambda lohi, d=1: f"{num(lohi[0], d)} to {num(lohi[1], d)}"
est_ci = lambda r, d=2: f"{r['exp']:.{d}f} ({r['low']:.{d}f} to {r['high']:.{d}f})"


def delay_share(c, labels):
    d = tab(c, "delay")
    return d.loc[d["delay"].isin(labels), "arrests"].sum() / d["arrests"].sum()
```

# Introduction

Crimes cluster in space and time beyond what stable hot spots explain. A
shooting is followed by a retaliatory shooting a few blocks away. Someone
breaking into cars works their way down a street tonight and comes back to
the same garage later in the week. Self-exciting point process models
capture this by letting each crime temporarily raise the rate of further
crimes nearby [@mohler2011; @mohler2014; @reinhart2018review], and they are
the engine behind a generation of crime forecasting tools [@mohler2015].

In those models every crime excites. Nothing in them represents the police
ending the chain. But the two stories above each have an obvious way to
stop: the person doing it gets arrested. In prior work we showed the
pattern with near repeat counts. For shootings, robberies, residential
burglaries, and thefts from motor vehicles in Dallas, crimes that resulted
in an arrest were 20% to 40% less likely to be followed by another crime
nearby in the following days [@wheeler2021chain]. Those were logistic
regressions for whether any follow-up crime occurred within a set distance
and time. A model of that form does not convert easily into a count of
crimes prevented, and it does not describe how the value of an arrest
changes with how quickly it is made.

This paper adds a term to the self-exciting model that does the opposite
of exciting. Each crime starts with the usual triggering kernel. If and
when the crime has an arrest, whatever triggering it had left is multiplied
by a factor $\kappa$. A value of $\kappa = 1$ means arrests change nothing,
$\kappa = 0$ means an arrest ends the chain, and values between are partial
dampening. Because the arrest enters the model at the time it happens, a
fast arrest removes more of the kernel than a slow one, and an arrest made
months later removes almost nothing. The fitted model converts directly
into the quantity of interest: the expected number of follow-on crimes each
arrest prevented, and the total across all arrests, including the crimes
those prevented crimes would have gone on to trigger.

I lay out the model and its likelihood, show in simulations that it
recovers the arrest effect and the count of crimes prevented, including when
the data come from an offender spree process it only approximates, and
apply it to shootings in Chicago, Illinois and car prowls (thefts from
motor vehicles) in Seattle, Washington. The method needs data that say
which crime had an arrest and when. Most open crime data lack this, and
these two cities publish it. Code, data, and paper source are at
https://github.com/apwheele/ArrestHawkes.

# Model

## A self-exciting model for crime

Crimes are points $(t_i, s_i)$, $i = 1, \dots, N$, with times $t_i$ in an
observation window $[0, T]$ and locations $s_i$ in the plane. A point
process is defined by its conditional intensity $\lambda(t, s)$, the
expected rate of crimes per unit time and area at $(t, s)$ given everything
that happened before $t$. The self-exciting (Hawkes) model
[@hawkes1971; @ogata1998; @mohler2011] is

$$
\lambda(t, s) = \mu(t, s) + \sum_{i:\, t_i < t} \theta_i \, g(t - t_i) \, h(s - s_i).
$$

The background $\mu(t, s)$ is crime that would happen regardless of recent
events: chronic hot spots, seasonality, long-run trends. Each past crime
adds a bump on top. The temporal kernel $g$ and the spatial kernel $h$ are
probability densities, so $\theta_i$ is the expected number of crimes
triggered directly by crime $i$, its productivity. The model has a
branching interpretation that I use throughout: every crime is either a
background event or the offspring of exactly one earlier crime, offspring
have offspring of their own, and if productivity averages $n < 1$ then one
background crime leads to $1/(1 - n)$ crimes in total, counting itself.

I let productivity depend on characteristics of the crime known at the
time, $\theta_i = \exp(x_i^\top \gamma)$, for example whether a shooting
injured someone. For the spatial kernel I use a bivariate Gaussian with
standard deviation $\sigma$. For the temporal kernel, write
$S(u) = \int_u^\infty g(v)\, dv$ for the share of a crime's triggering that is
still to come $u$ days after it. I fit two forms and choose by likelihood:
the exponential, $g(u) = \omega e^{-\omega u}$ with
$S(u) = e^{-\omega u}$, and a power law (the Omori law of earthquake
aftershocks, @ogata1988), $g(u) = (p - 1)\, c^{\,p-1} (u + c)^{-p}$ with
$S(u) = (1 + u/c)^{-(p - 1)}$, which has a sharper peak and a longer tail.

## Arrests dampen what triggering is left

Let $a_i$ be the time of the arrest for crime $i$, with $a_i = \infty$ if
there is none, and let $A_i(t) = 1$ if $a_i < t$ and 0 otherwise. The model
with arrest dampening is

$$
\lambda(t, s) = \mu(t, s) + \sum_{i:\, t_i < t} \theta_i \, \kappa_i^{A_i(t)} \, g(t - t_i) \, h(s - s_i).
$$

Before the arrest, crime $i$ excites as usual. From the arrest on, its
kernel is multiplied by $\kappa_i \ge 0$ (@fig-schematic). I mostly use a
single $\kappa$, but the multiplier can depend on characteristics of the
arrest, $\kappa_i = \exp(z_i^\top \beta)$, for example whether the person
was booked into jail or released. The intensity only uses arrests made
before $t$, so it is a valid conditional intensity, and it stays
non-negative for any $\kappa_i \ge 0$. General inhibition in Hawkes
processes, where events subtract from the intensity, needs a nonlinear link
to keep the intensity positive and complicates estimation
[@bonnet2021]; scaling a crime's own kernel avoids that.

```{python}
#| label: fig-schematic
#| fig-cap: "The arrest term. A crime triggers follow-on crimes at a rate that decays with time (dashed). An arrest multiplies the remaining rate by $\\kappa$ (here 0.3), and the shaded area is the expected number of follow-on crimes the arrest prevents. An arrest made sooner removes more."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.1))
plots.schematic(ax)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The expected number of direct offspring of a crime arrested after a delay
$d_i = a_i - t_i$ is the full-strength part before the arrest plus the
dampened part after,

$$
m_i = \theta_i \left[ 1 - S(d_i) \right] + \theta_i \kappa_i S(d_i)
    = \theta_i \left[ 1 - (1 - \kappa_i)\, S(d_i) \right],
$$

so the arrest removes $\theta_i (1 - \kappa_i) S(d_i)$ direct offspring.
With the exponential kernel that is $\theta_i (1 - \kappa_i) e^{-\omega d_i}$:
an arrest at the scene ($d_i = 0$) removes the share $1 - \kappa_i$ of
everything the crime would have triggered, and each $\log(2)/\omega$ days of
delay cuts what the arrest can prevent in half.

What $\kappa$ picks up depends on the crime. For a spree, where follow-on
crimes are the same person continuing, the arrest incapacitates and
$\kappa$ should be near zero if the right person is in custody. For
retaliatory violence the follow-on crime is committed by someone else, and
an arrest may or may not satisfy the other side [@papachristos2009], so
$\kappa$ could be anywhere, in principle even above one.

## Why the arrest has to enter at the time it happens

A simpler model treats an eventual arrest as a fixed characteristic of the
crime, the way @park2021 let gang crimes that received a violence
interruption response have their own triggering rate. With arrests that is
wrong in a way that matters. The crime's follow-on crimes
that came before the arrest could not have been affected by it, but the
fixed-mark model counts them as evidence about $\kappa$. This is the
immortal time bias of survival analysis [@suissa2008], and here it runs in
a known direction: it pulls the estimate of $\kappa$ toward one. It is
worse than that when arrests clear several crimes at once. If a car prowler
is caught on the third night and the arrest clears all three reports, the
first two crimes are "arrested" crimes that each had a follow-on crime, and
the fixed-mark model reads arrests as failing to stop anything. Entering
the arrest as a change at time $a_i$ uses only what came after it.

## Likelihood

The log-likelihood of a point process on $[0, T]$ is the sum of the log
intensity at the observed events minus the integral of the intensity,

$$
\ell = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \log \lambda(t_j, s_j) - \int_0^T \!\! \int \lambda(t, s)\, ds\, dt .
$$

The integral has a closed form. Let $c_i = \min(a_i, T) - t_i$ be the time
crime $i$ spends at full strength inside the window. Ignoring the small
part of the spatial kernels that falls outside the city,

$$
\int_0^T \!\! \int \lambda \, ds\, dt = \int_0^T \!\! \int \mu \, ds\, dt
 + \sum_{i=1}^{N} \theta_i \left\{ \left[ 1 - S(c_i) \right] + \kappa_i \left[ S(c_i) - S(T - t_i) \right] \right\} .
$$

Each term is the expected offspring of crime $i$ in the window: the share
due before the arrest at full strength, and the share due between the
arrest and $T$ multiplied by $\kappa_i$. For a crime with no arrest by $T$
the second piece is zero. The arrest times are treated as given. This is a
partial likelihood: I do not model when arrests happen, only what happens to
the crime rate after they do.

The parameters are estimated by maximizing $\ell$. I supply the analytic
gradient and use L-BFGS, with standard errors from the inverse of the
numerically differentiated Hessian. The likelihood can have more than one
local maximum (a short, tight kernel or a long, wide one), so each fit
starts from several kernel scales and keeps the best. The test of
$\kappa = 1$ is a likelihood ratio test against the model without the arrest
term. When $\kappa$ is near zero its log is poorly described by a normal
distribution, so I report profile likelihood intervals: the values of
$\kappa$ whose best-fitting likelihood is within 1.92 of the maximum.

## Background

The background is separable, $\mu(t, s) = \nu(t)\, b(s)$. The temporal part
$\nu(t)$ is a step function with a free level for each quarter, which
absorbs trends and seasonality that would otherwise be read as contagion.
The spatial part $b(s)$ is a kernel density estimate built from the crime
locations themselves, with a variable bandwidth as in @mohler2011: each
crime contributes a Gaussian whose standard deviation is the distance to its
$k$-th nearest neighbor (no smaller than 40 meters), so the surface is
sharp where crime is dense and smooth where it is sparse. The density at crime $j$ leaves out crime $j$'s
own kernel. A smoother background leaves more clustering for the triggering
term to explain, so the choice of $k$ matters for $\theta$. I choose $k$ by
the likelihood and report how the results move across values.

## Crimes prevented

The direct offspring removed by the arrests made in the window are

$$
D = \sum_{i:\, a_i \le T} \theta_i (1 - \kappa_i) \left[ S(c_i) - S(T - t_i) \right].
$$

Each of those crimes would have triggered others. Let
$n_0 = \frac{1}{N} \sum_i \theta_i$ be the average productivity with no
arrest effect and $n_1 = n_0 - D/N$ the average productivity given the
arrests made. With $B$ background crimes, the expected totals are
$B/(1 - n_0)$ without the arrest effect and $N = B/(1 - n_1)$ with it, and
the difference is

$$
P = \frac{B}{1 - n_0} - \frac{B}{1 - n_1} = \frac{D}{1 - n_0} .
$$

This is the estimate of crimes prevented: the number of additional crimes
expected had the same arrests been made with no effect on triggering. For a
single arrest of an average crime made after a delay $d$ it is
$\bar\theta (1 - \kappa) S(d) / (1 - n_0)$, which gives a curve of crimes
prevented against time to arrest.

$P$ is an expected count. The number of crimes actually prevented is
random even if the parameters were known, because how many crimes a crime
triggers is random. The removed direct offspring are Poisson with mean $D$,
and each would have started a family of crimes whose size has mean
$1/(1 - n_0)$ and variance $n_0/(1 - n_0)^3$, so the realized count has
variance $D \left[ n_0/(1 - n_0)^3 + 1/(1 - n_0)^2 \right]$ around $P$. The
intervals I report for crimes prevented are prediction intervals for the
realized count. They start from the interval for $P$ implied by the profile
likelihood for $\kappa$ (refitting the other parameters at each end) and
widen each side by this process variance, combining the two in quadrature.

## What has to hold

The model compares what follows arrested crimes, after their arrests, with
what follows other crimes at the same lag. Reading $\kappa$ as the effect of
the arrest needs three things. First, crimes that get arrests must not
differ in productivity for other reasons, given the covariates in
$\theta_i$. A domestic shooting is both easier to clear and less likely to
spark retaliation, which would make arrests look more effective than they
are; a prolific offender who is eventually caught would make them look less
effective. Second, the arrest must not have been caused by the absence of
follow-on crimes or the reverse, beyond the time ordering the model already
respects. Third, the arrest linked to the crime in the data must be the
relevant one. An arrest that takes an offender off the street prevents that
person's future crimes whichever report it is filed under, and the model
only credits it against the crime it is linked to.

# Simulations

I check the method on simulated cities where the number of crimes prevented
is known. Each world is a 10 km square observed for four years. Background
crimes arrive at two per day, 60% in 25 hot spots and the rest uniformly.
Replaying the same random draws with the arrest effect switched off gives
the crimes that would have occurred, and the difference from the crimes
that did occur is the true number prevented. There are six scenarios and
`{python} n_rep` worlds each, averaging
`{python} num(round(simsum["n"].mean(), -2))` crimes and
`{python} num(round(simsum["arrests"].mean(), -1))` arrests per world.

The first four draw from the model itself, with productivity
$\theta = 0.35$, an exponential kernel with a mean of two days
($\omega = 0.5$), $\sigma = 120$ meters, and 15% of crimes arrested.

- *Model.* $\kappa = 0.3$. Forty percent of arrests are at the scene and
  the rest follow after an exponential delay averaging three days.
- *No arrest effect.* The same with $\kappa = 1$.
- *Late arrests.* $\kappa = 0.3$ and no arrests at the scene; delays
  average two days, as long as the triggering lasts.
- *Confounded.* $\kappa = 0.3$. Thirty percent of crimes have a trait that
  doubles their productivity and quadruples their odds of arrest.

The last two do not come from the model. They simulate offenders. A spree
starts as a background crime; after each crime the offender commits another
with probability 0.45 after an exponential gap averaging two days, a short
distance away. Each crime leads to an arrest with probability 0.15, half at
the scene and half after a delay averaging two days, and an arrest removes
every later crime in the spree.

- *Sprees.* The arrest is recorded against the crime that led to it.
- *Sprees, earlier crimes cleared.* The arrest also clears 70% of the
  offender's earlier crimes, recorded with the same arrest time.

For each world I fit the model with the arrest entering at its time, and the
fixed-mark version that treats an eventual arrest as a characteristic of the
crime. In the confounded scenario I also fit the model with the trait as a
productivity covariate.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-sim
#| tbl-cap: "Simulation results. Median estimate of $\\kappa$, the share of worlds rejecting $\\kappa = 1$ at the 5% level, mean true and estimated crimes prevented, and coverage of the 95% intervals (profile likelihood for $\\kappa$, prediction interval for crimes prevented; models with the arrest at its time only)."
rows = []
for scen in SCEN:
    for meth in METH:
        if (scen, meth) not in simsum.index:
            continue
        r = simsum.loc[(scen, meth)]
        f = lambda v: "" if np.isnan(v) else pct(v)
        rows.append({
            "Scenario": SCEN[scen], "Method": METH[meth], "True $\\kappa$": f"{r['ktrue']:.1f}",
            "Median $\\kappa$": f"{r['kmed']:.2f}", "Reject $\\kappa$ = 1": pct(r["reject"]), "Cover $\\kappa$": f(r["cover_k"]),
            "Prevented, true": num(r["truth"]), "Prevented, est.": num(r["est"]), "Cover prevented": f(r["cover"]),
        })
show(pd.DataFrame(rows), left=2)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-sim
#| fig-cap: "Estimated minus true crimes prevented in each simulated world (points) and the median (bar), by scenario and method. Zero is a perfect estimate."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(8.2, 5.2))
short = {"dynamic": "At its\ntime", "static": "Fixed\nmark", "dynamic + covariate": "At its time\n+ covariate"}
colors = {"dynamic": plots.BLUE, "static": plots.ORANGE, "dynamic + covariate": plots.AQUA}
for ax, scen in zip(axes.ravel(), SCEN):
    g = sim[sim["scenario"] == scen]
    ms = [m for m in METH if m in set(g["method"])]
    plots.sim_strip(ax, g, "err", 0.0, ms, [short[m] for m in ms], [colors[m] for m in ms], "")
    ax.set_title(f"{SCEN[scen]} (true mean {num(g['truth'].mean())})", fontsize=9.5)
for ax in axes[:, 0]:
    ax.set_ylabel("Estimate minus truth (crimes)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

@tbl-sim and @fig-sim give the results. When the data come from the model,
the estimate of $\kappa$ is centered on the truth (median
`{python} f"{SS('model', 'dynamic', 'kmed'):.2f}"` against 0.3), the test
rejects no effect in `{python} pct(SS('model', 'dynamic', 'reject'))` of
worlds, and the estimate of crimes prevented averages
`{python} num(SS('model', 'dynamic', 'est'))` against a true
`{python} num(SS('model', 'dynamic', 'truth'))`. With no arrest effect the
test rejects in `{python} pct(SS('null', 'dynamic', 'reject'))` of worlds,
close to its nominal 5%. Profile intervals for $\kappa$ cover in
`{python} pct(SS('model', 'dynamic', 'cover_k'))` of worlds and the
intervals for crimes prevented in
`{python} pct(SS('model', 'dynamic', 'cover'))`.

The fixed-mark model is biased in every scenario where arrests take time.
Its median $\kappa$ is `{python} f"{SS('model', 'static', 'kmed'):.2f}"` in
the first scenario and `{python} f"{SS('late', 'static', 'kmed'):.2f}"`
when all arrests are late, and it finds
`{python} pct(1 - SS('late', 'static', 'est') / SS('late', 'static', 'truth'))`
fewer crimes prevented than there were. When one arrest clears a string of
earlier crimes it fails entirely: median $\kappa$ of
`{python} f"{SS('spree_clear', 'static', 'kmed'):.2f}"`, in a world where
every arrest ends a spree.

Confounding does what it should. Leaving out a trait that raises both
productivity and the chance of arrest makes arrested crimes look more
productive, so $\kappa$ is overstated (median
`{python} f"{SS('confounded', 'dynamic', 'kmed'):.2f}"`) and crimes
prevented understated. With the trait in the model the bias is gone
(`{python} f"{SS('confounded', 'dynamic + covariate', 'kmed'):.2f}"`).

In the spree worlds the model is only an approximation: an offender commits
at most one next crime, where the model's crimes have a Poisson number of
offspring. It still reads the arrest correctly. The estimate of $\kappa$
goes to zero (median
`{python} f"{SS('spree', 'dynamic', 'kmed'):.3f}"`), and estimated crimes
prevented average `{python} num(SS('spree', 'dynamic', 'est'))` against a
true `{python} num(SS('spree', 'dynamic', 'truth'))`, an underestimate of
`{python} pct(1 - SS('spree', 'dynamic', 'est') / SS('spree', 'dynamic', 'truth'))`.
When arrests also clear earlier crimes the estimate of $\kappa$ still goes
to zero, but crimes prevented are overstated by
`{python} pct(SS('spree_clear', 'dynamic', 'est') / SS('spree_clear', 'dynamic', 'truth') - 1)`
(`{python} num(SS('spree_clear', 'dynamic', 'est'))` against
`{python} num(SS('spree_clear', 'dynamic', 'truth'))`). Each earlier crime
cleared by the arrest is credited with removing what was left of its own
kernel, although the one arrest had already ended the spree. Where an
arrest clears a string of crimes it should be attached to the last of them.
In both spree scenarios the intervals, which take the model as given, are
too narrow: they cover the true count in
`{python} pct(SS('spree', 'dynamic', 'cover'))` and
`{python} pct(SS('spree_clear', 'dynamic', 'cover'))` of worlds.

# Data

The model needs, for each crime, a time, a location, and the time of the
arrest if there was one, and the arrests have to be complete enough that
an unarrested crime really had no arrest. Few police departments publish
that. Our earlier near repeat analysis used Dallas [@wheeler2021chain], but
its public arrest table is missing about half of the arrests its incident
table reports (below). I use Chicago for shootings and Seattle for car
prowls. In both, every arrest is tied to the crime by its case number and
has a date and time. The data were downloaded in November 2026.

*Shootings: Chicago, Illinois.* The city's violence reduction data list
every victim of a homicide or non-fatal shooting, with the case number, the
date and time, whether the victim was shot, and a location moved from the
address but kept on the same block [@cpdvictims]. A shooting incident here
is a case number with at least one gunshot victim, fatal if any victim
died, from January 2016 through June 2026. That gives
`{python} num(meta["shootings"]["n"])` incidents, of which
`{python} num(meta["shootings"]["fatal"])` were fatal; all have
coordinates. Whether a shooting was fatal is a productivity covariate. The
arrest table has one row per arrest with the date and time, the charges,
and, for about 70% of arrests, the case number of the crime [@cpdarrests].
I link each shooting to the earliest arrest under its case number. An
arrest under the same case number is not always of the shooter: of the
linked shootings, `{python} pct(1 - meta["shootings_violent"]["arrested"] / meta["shootings"]["arrested"])`
have only arrests on gun possession, drug, or other charges, which may be
of a victim or bystander. The main analysis counts any arrest under the
case number, and a sensitivity analysis counts only arrests with a violent
charge or on a warrant.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-check
#| tbl-cap: "Share of Chicago shooting incidents with an arrest in the open data, against arrest rates published from police records. Published figures count victims or cases and were measured soon after the year ended; the open data figures are as of November 2026."
ys = meta["shootings"]["arrest_share_by_year"]
yv = meta["shootings_violent"]["arrest_share_by_year"]
rows = [
    {"Year": "2022", "Shootings": "Fatal", "Open data, any arrest": pct(ys["2022"]["fatal"]),
     "Open data, violent charge": pct(yv["2022"]["fatal"]), "Published": "27% (CBS Chicago, from CPD records)"},
    {"Year": "2023", "Shootings": "Fatal", "Open data, any arrest": pct(ys["2023"]["fatal"]),
     "Open data, violent charge": pct(yv["2023"]["fatal"]), "Published": "17%, first 10 months (CBS Chicago)"},
    {"Year": "2021-2024", "Shootings": "Fatal", "Open data, any arrest": pct(sum(ys[y]["fatal"] for y in ("2021", "2022", "2023", "2024")) / 4),
     "Open data, violent charge": pct(sum(yv[y]["fatal"] for y in ("2021", "2022", "2023", "2024")) / 4),
     "Published": "25% cleared by arrest, year not stated (Sun-Times)"},
    {"Year": "2024", "Shootings": "Non-fatal", "Open data, any arrest": pct(ys["2024"]["injury"]),
     "Open data, violent charge": pct(yv["2024"]["injury"]), "Published": "141 of about 2,300 victims, 6% (Sun-Times)"},
    {"Year": "2018-2024", "Shootings": "Non-fatal",
     "Open data, any arrest": pct(sum(ys[str(y)]["injury"] for y in range(2018, 2025)) / 7),
     "Open data, violent charge": pct(sum(yv[str(y)]["injury"] for y in range(2018, 2025)) / 7),
     "Published": "1,200 of more than 19,000 victims, about 6% (Sun-Times)"},
]
show(pd.DataFrame(rows), left=2)
```

@tbl-check compares the arrest share in the open data with arrest rates
reported from police records by CBS Chicago, which obtained them under the
Freedom of Information Act [@cbs2024], and the Chicago Sun-Times
[@suntimes2025]. Both separate arrests from the much larger number of
cases closed by exceptional means. The open data land in the same range:
about one in five fatal shootings and one in fifteen non-fatal shootings
had an arrest. The published non-fatal figures count victims, and an
incident can have several, so per incident they would be somewhat higher.

*Car prowls: Seattle, Washington.* The Seattle Police Department's crime
table has one row per offense with the report number, the date and time of
the offense, and a location masked to the hundred block [@spdcrime]. Its
arrest table starts in 2019 and has one row per arrest charge with the date
and time of the arrest, the report number of the case, and the type of
arrest [@spdarrest]. Car prowls are offenses coded theft from motor
vehicle, from January 2019 through June 2026, which leaves four months for
late-entered arrests. The offense time is the start of the period the
victim reports, and for a car broken into overnight that can be off by
hours. In both cities I link each case to the earliest arrest with the
same number, and an arrest logged shortly before the offense time
(`{python} meta["shootings"]["arrest_before_offense"]` shootings,
`{python} meta["carprowl"]["arrest_before_offense"]` car prowls) is
treated as made at the scene.

*Cities that did not work.* Seattle also flags shootings, but its public
file redacts the location of nearly all fatal shootings. In Dallas, the
incident table's own case status says that 36% to 60% of gun homicides
each year were cleared by arrest, but only half of the incidents with that
status appear in the public arrest table, the only source of an arrest
date, and only a few percent of gun homicides do. In Baltimore, arrests
that carry an incident number link to about 9% of shootings, against a
clearance rate the department reports at over 50%. Philadelphia publishes
shootings with exact times and locations but arrests only as daily counts
by area; its arrests can be found in Pennsylvania court dockets by incident
number, but the court portal limits searches to about one a minute. Other
large cities either publish no arrest table with a case number or
anonymize the case number.

Both cities publish the block and not the address, so many cases share
identical coordinates, which a continuous spatial kernel cannot handle
(the likelihood is unbounded as $\sigma$ goes to zero). I add Gaussian
noise with a standard deviation of `{python} num(cp["jitter"])` meters to
each coordinate, about the spread of a uniform position along a block, and
check how much results depend on the random draw.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-data
#| tbl-cap: "The two samples."
rows = []
PERIOD = {"shootings": "Jan 2016 to Jun 2026", "carprowl": "Jan 2019 to Jun 2026"}
DAY = ["at the offense time", "within 1 hour", "1 to 6 hours", "6 to 24 hours"]
WEEK = ["7 to 30 days", "30 to 180 days", "over 180 days"]
for c in CRIMES:
    s, m = S[c], meta[c]
    rows.append({
        "": CNAME[c], "Period": PERIOD[c], "Cases": num(m["reports"]), "With location": num(m["n"]),
        "With an arrest": f"{num(m['arrested'])} ({pct(m['arrested'] / m['n'], 1)})",
        "Arrest within an hour": pct(delay_share(c, FAST)),
        "Arrest after a week or more": pct(delay_share(c, WEEK)),
    })
show(pd.DataFrame(rows), left=2)
```

@tbl-data describes the two samples. Arrests are uncommon:
`{python} pct(meta["shootings"]["arrested"] / meta["shootings"]["n"], 1)` of
shootings and `{python} pct(meta["carprowl"]["arrested"] / meta["carprowl"]["n"], 1)`
of car prowls have one. The timing differs.
`{python} pct(delay_share("carprowl", FAST))` of car prowl arrests are within
an hour of the offense, people caught in the act. Shooting arrests are
mostly the product of an investigation:
`{python} pct(delay_share("shootings", FAST))` come within an hour and
`{python} pct(delay_share("shootings", WEEK))` a week or more later.
Seattle's arrest table also records the type of arrest.
`{python} pct(1 - meta["carprowl"]["booked"] / meta["carprowl"]["arrested"])`
of car prowl arrests do not end with the person booked into jail (they are
identified and released, cited, or referred for charges), which lets the
model ask whether custody is what matters.

```{python}
#| label: fig-followon
#| fig-cap: "Later crimes of the same type within 200 meters, per earlier crime per day, by time since the earlier crime. Gray: earlier crimes with no arrest. Blue: earlier crimes with an arrest within a day. The last bin (one to four months later) is the long-run rate at those places. Dashed lines are what the fitted model of the Results section implies: the long-run rate plus the direct triggering expected in each bin, multiplied by $\\kappa$ after an arrest."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.2, 3.6))
for ax, c in zip(axes, CRIMES):
    plots.followon_panel(ax, tab(c, "followon"), CNAME[c], summary=S[c])
axes[0].set_ylabel("Follow-on crimes per crime per day")
axes[1].legend(loc="upper right")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
fo = {c: tab(c, "followon").set_index(["group", "lag_from"]) for c in CRIMES}
FASTG = "arrest within a day"
fo_rate = lambda c, g, lag: fo[c].loc[(g, lag), "rate"]
fo_pairs = lambda c, g, lag: int(fo[c].loc[(g, lag), "pairs"])
fo_parents = lambda c, g: int(fo[c].loc[(g, 0.0), "parents"])
# pairs in the first day, and the number the long-run rate would give
day1 = lambda c, g: fo_pairs(c, g, 0.0) + fo_pairs(c, g, 0.25)
day1_expected = lambda c, g: fo_rate(c, g, 28.0) * fo_parents(c, g)
```

@fig-followon shows the pattern the model has to explain, before any
model. For each crime I count later crimes of the same type within 200
meters and divide by the time at risk. In the six hours after a car prowl
with no arrest, further car prowls nearby come at
`{python} f"{fo_rate('carprowl', 'no arrest', 0.0) / fo_rate('carprowl', 'no arrest', 28.0):.1f}"`
times the long-run rate at those places, and the excess decays over the
following days. After a car prowl with an arrest within a day the spike is
mostly gone
(`{python} f"{fo_rate('carprowl', FASTG, 0.0) / fo_rate('carprowl', FASTG, 28.0):.1f}"`
times the long-run rate, from
`{python} fo_pairs('carprowl', FASTG, 0.0)` pairs).

Chicago shootings show the same shape on a smaller scale. In the six hours
after a shooting with no arrest, further shootings within 200 meters come
at `{python} f"{fo_rate('shootings', 'no arrest', 0.0) / fo_rate('shootings', 'no arrest', 28.0):.1f}"`
times the long-run rate, and in the first day there are
`{python} num(day1('shootings', 'no arrest'))` such follow-on shootings
where the long-run rate implies
`{python} num(day1_expected('shootings', 'no arrest'))`. After the
`{python} num(fo_parents('shootings', FASTG))` shootings with an arrest
within a day, `{python} day1('shootings', FASTG)` followed nearby in the
next day, where `{python} num(day1_expected('shootings', FASTG), 1)` would
be expected at the long-run rate.

# Results

```{python}
#| label: tbl-models
#| tbl-cap: "Model comparison. Log-likelihood, number of parameters, and AIC (lower is better)."
rows = []
for c in CRIMES:
    m = tab(c, "models")
    for _, r in m.iterrows():
        rows.append({"": CNAME[c] if r["model"] == m["model"].iloc[0] else "", "Model": r["model"],
                     "Log-likelihood": num(r["loglik"], 1), "Parameters": int(r["npar"]), "AIC": num(r["aic"], 1)})
show(pd.DataFrame(rows), left=2)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-est
#| tbl-cap: "Estimates from the arrest dampening model, with 95% intervals. The interval for $\\kappa$ is from the profile likelihood; the others are Wald intervals computed on the log scale."
def est_rows(c):
    s = S[c]
    co = tab(c, "coef").query("model == 'main'").set_index("name")
    kp = s["kernel_par"]
    out = {
        "Kernel": s["kernel_name"].capitalize(),
        "Background neighbors k": str(s["k_nn"]),
        "Productivity $\\theta$": est_ci(s["theta"], 3),
        "Fatal shooting multiplier on $\\theta$": est_ci(s["covariate_effect"], 2) if s["covariate_effect"] else "",
        "Arrest multiplier $\\kappa$": f"{s['kappa']['exp']:.2f} ({s['kappa_profile'][0]:.2f} to {s['kappa_profile'][1]:.2f})",
        "Test of $\\kappa$ = 1, p-value": pval(s["lr_arrest"]["p"]),
        "Median lag to a triggered crime": (f"{kp['median_days']:.1f} days" if kp["median_days"] >= 1
                                             else f"{kp['median_days'] * 24:.1f} hours"),
        "Spatial spread $\\sigma$ (meters)": est_ci(s["sigma"], 0),
        "Share of crimes triggered": pct(s["triggered_share"], 1),
    }
    return out


e = {c: est_rows(c) for c in CRIMES}
show(pd.DataFrame({"": list(e["shootings"]), CNAME["shootings"]: list(e["shootings"].values()),
                   CNAME["carprowl"]: list(e["carprowl"].values())}))
```

For each crime type I fit both temporal kernels with the background's
nearest-neighbor count $k$ at 5, 10, 15, and 30, and take the combination
with the highest likelihood (@tbl-grid in the appendix has all of them).
@tbl-models compares models at that choice and @tbl-est gives the
estimates.

## Car prowls

Car prowls are self-exciting, modestly. The self-exciting model improves
the log-likelihood over the background alone by
`{python} num(tab("carprowl", "models").set_index("model").loc["Self-exciting, no arrest effect", "loglik"] - tab("carprowl", "models").set_index("model").loc["Poisson background", "loglik"])`
with a handful of parameters, and
`{python} pct(cp["triggered_share"], 1)` of car prowls are attributed to an
earlier one. The triggering is fast and local. The power law kernel fits
far better than the exponential, half of triggered car prowls come within
`{python} f"{cp['kernel_par']['median_days'] * 24:.0f}"` hours of the one
that triggered them, and the spatial spread is
`{python} num(cp["sigma"]["exp"])` meters, about a block. This is what a
spree looks like.

Arrests cut it off. The estimate of $\kappa$ is
`{python} f"{cp['kappa']['exp']:.2f}"` (95% profile interval
`{python} f"{cp['kappa_profile'][0]:.2f}"` to
`{python} f"{cp['kappa_profile'][1]:.2f}"`): after an arrest, a car prowl
triggers about `{python} pct(1 - cp['kappa']['exp'])` fewer follow-on car
prowls than it otherwise would have from that point. The likelihood ratio
test against no arrest effect has a p-value
`{python} pval(cp["lr_arrest"]["p"])` (@fig-profile). Because nearly all
car prowl arrests are made within the hour, the fixed-mark model gives a
similar answer here
(`{python} f"{cp['kappa_static']['exp']:.2f}"`); the two would diverge in
data with more follow-up arrests.

```{python}
#| label: fig-profile
#| fig-cap: "Profile likelihood for the arrest multiplier $\\kappa$: twice the drop in log-likelihood from its maximum. Values below the dotted line are inside the 95% interval. The dashed line marks no arrest effect."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.2, 3.1), sharey=True)
for ax, c in zip(axes, CRIMES):
    plots.profile_panel(ax, S[c], CNAME[c])
axes[0].set_ylabel("2 x drop in log-likelihood")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Does it matter whether the person goes to jail?
`{python} num(cp["booked"])` of the `{python} num(cp["arrests"])` car prowl
arrests ended in a booking; the rest were identified and released, cited,
or referred for charges. Letting $\kappa$ differ between the two gives
`{python} f"{cp['kappa_not_booked']['exp']:.2f}"` for arrests without a
booking and an estimate at zero for arrests with one, but the likelihood
ratio test of a difference has a p-value of
`{python} pval(cp["lr_booked"]["p"])`. The data cannot tell the two apart.
Both kinds of arrest are followed by far fewer car prowls than no arrest,
which fits an offender who stops for the night once caught, in custody or
not.

## Shootings

```{python}
shv = json.load(open(R / "models" / "shootings_violent_summary.json"))
sh_models = tab("shootings", "models").set_index("model")["loglik"]
fast_share = delay_share("shootings", FAST)
```

Chicago shootings are self-exciting, but only slightly. The self-exciting
model improves the log-likelihood over the background alone by
`{python} num(sh_models["Self-exciting, no arrest effect"] - sh_models["Poisson background"])`,
and it attributes `{python} pct(sh["triggered_share"], 1)` of shooting
incidents to an earlier one, with productivity
`{python} f"{sh['theta']['exp']:.3f}"`. The triggering is fast and spread
out: half of triggered shootings come within
`{python} f"{sh['kernel_par']['median_days'] * 24 * 60:.0f}"` minutes of the
earlier one, and the spatial spread is
`{python} num(sh["sigma"]["exp"])` meters. That looks less like repeat
shootings at one address than like an exchange of gunfire, or a retaliation
the same night, a few blocks away. Fatal shootings trigger fewer follow-on
shootings than non-fatal ones (multiplier
`{python} est_ci(sh["covariate_effect"], 2)`). This fits @loeffler2018, who
found with acoustic gunshot detection data that gun violence does spread,
but only slightly. One caution on scope: an incident with several victims
counts once here, and retaliation that follows social ties across the city
[@papachristos2009; @green2017] would not show up as clustering in space.

The data cannot tell whether arrests stop follow-on shootings. The estimate
of $\kappa$ is `{python} f"{sh['kappa']['exp']:.2f}"`, with a 95% profile
interval of `{python} f"{sh['kappa_profile'][0]:.2f}"` to
`{python} f"{sh['kappa_profile'][1]:.2f}"` that includes no effect
(p-value `{python} pval(sh["lr_arrest"]["p"])`). Counting only arrests with
a violent charge or on a warrant gives
`{python} f"{shv['kappa']['exp']:.2f}"`
(`{python} f"{shv['kappa_profile'][0]:.2f}"` to
`{python} f"{shv['kappa_profile'][1]:.2f}"`, p-value
`{python} pval(shv["lr_arrest"]["p"])`), and the estimate moves with the
random draw used to unmask locations
(`{python} " and ".join(f"{j['kappa']:.2f}" for j in sh["jitter_check"])`
with two other draws). The reason is in the timing. With half of the
triggering over within about an hour, only an arrest in that hour can
remove much of it, and only `{python} pct(fast_share)` of shooting arrests
come that fast; the median arrest is
`{python} num(sh["median_delay_days"])` days after the shooting. The
`{python} num(sh["arrests"])` shootings with an arrest by the end of June
2026 would trigger about
`{python} num(sh["arrests"] * sh["theta"]["exp"])` shootings between them
with no arrest effect, most of them before any arrest.

## Crimes prevented

```{python}
#| label: tbl-prevented
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated crimes prevented by arrests (Chicago shootings January 2016 through June 2026, Seattle car prowls January 2019 through June 2026). Direct: follow-on crimes of the arrested crimes. Total: including the crimes those would have triggered. Intervals are 95% prediction intervals."
rows = []
for c in CRIMES:
    s = S[c]
    p = s["prevented"]
    rows.append({
        "": CNAME[c], "Crimes": num(s["n"]), "Arrests": num(s["arrests"]),
        "Prevented, direct": num(p["direct"], 1),
        "Prevented, total": f"{num(p['total'], 1)} ({ci(s['prevented_prediction'])})",
        "Per 100 arrests": num(100 * p["per_arrest"], 1),
        "Share of crimes": pct(p["share"], 2),
    })
show(pd.DataFrame(rows))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-curve
#| fig-cap: "Estimated crimes prevented by one arrest, by how long after the crime the arrest is made (follow-on crimes and their descendants; bands are the estimates at the two ends of the 95% profile interval for $\\kappa$)."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.2, 3.5))
for ax, c in zip(axes, CRIMES):
    plots.curve_panel(ax, tab(c, "curve"), CNAME[c])
axes[0].set_ylabel("Crimes prevented per arrest")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

@tbl-prevented turns the estimates into counts. The
`{python} num(cp["arrests"])` car prowl arrests prevented an estimated
`{python} num(cp["prevented"]["total"])` car prowls (95% interval
`{python} ci(cp["prevented_prediction"], 0)`), about
`{python} num(100 * cp["prevented"]["per_arrest"], 0)` for every 100 arrests.
The effect of an arrest is large in relative terms and small in absolute
terms, and the reason is in the two numbers that multiply together. A car
prowl triggers `{python} f"{cp['theta']['exp']:.2f}"` others on average, so
that is the most an arrest at the scene can prevent directly, and only
`{python} pct(meta["carprowl"]["arrested"] / meta["carprowl"]["n"], 1)` of
car prowls have an arrest. Against
`{python} num(cp["n"])` car prowls in the period, the chains broken by
arrest are `{python} pct(cp["prevented"]["share"], 2)`.

@fig-curve shows how fast the value of an arrest decays. For car prowls an
arrest at the scene prevents about
`{python} f"{tab('carprowl', 'curve')['prevented'].iloc[0]:.3f}"` crimes; one
made a day later prevents
`{python} f"{np.interp(1.0, tab('carprowl', 'curve')['delay'], tab('carprowl', 'curve')['prevented']):.3f}"`,
because by then
`{python} pct(1 - np.interp(1.0, tab('carprowl', 'kernel')['delay'], tab('carprowl', 'kernel')['remaining']))`
of the follow-on crimes have already happened. For shootings the estimate is
`{python} num(sh["prevented"]["total"])` shootings prevented in ten and a
half years, with an interval (`{python} ci(sh["prevented_prediction"], 0)`)
that includes zero, and the curve falls to nothing within a few hours.

These counts are only the crimes prevented through this channel: the
short-run chain that follows a specific crime. An arrest that incapacitates
a prolific offender for months, or deters others, prevents crimes the
triggering kernel never sees.

## Checks

The dashed lines in @fig-followon are a check on fit: the follow-on rates
the fitted model implies, against the raw rates. For car prowls the model
reproduces the spike in the first six hours and its absence after an
arrest. It puts
`{python} f"{fo_rate('carprowl', 'no arrest', 0.0):.2f}"` observed against
`{python} f"{S['carprowl']['prevented']['n0'] * (1 - np.exp(-200**2 / (2 * cp['sigma']['exp']**2))) * (1 - plots.kernel_survival(cp, 0.25)) / 0.25 + fo_rate('carprowl', 'no arrest', 28.0):.2f}"`
implied in that first bin, and it is low over the next two weeks, where the
raw rate stays a little above the long-run rate longer than a single kernel
allows. For shootings the model accounts for only part of the excess in
the first six hours within 200 meters, since its fitted spatial spread is
wider than that. The usual residual check for point processes, rescaling time by
the fitted citywide intensity so that gaps between crimes should be
Exponential(1) [@ogata1988; @brown2002], is not informative here.
`{python} pct(cp["on_the_hour"])` of car prowl offense times are recorded
on the hour and `{python} pct(cp["tie_share"])` of car prowls share a
timestamp with the one before, so the residuals fail in the same
way for every model (Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance
`{python} f"{S['carprowl']['residuals']['main']['ks']:.2f}"` for the
arrest model and
`{python} f"{S['carprowl']['residuals']['Poisson background']['ks']:.2f}"`
for the background alone). Crimes with identical recorded times also
cannot be ordered, so neither counts as triggering the other, which makes
the estimate of $\theta$ conservative.

The car prowl estimates do not depend on the random draw used to unmask
locations: with two other draws $\kappa$ is
`{python} " and ".join(f"{j['kappa']:.2f}" for j in cp["jitter_check"])`
and crimes prevented
`{python} " and ".join(num(j["prevented"]) for j in cp["jitter_check"])`.
They do depend, as expected, on how smooth the background is (@tbl-grid).
A smoother background (larger $k$) hands more clustering to the triggering
term, raising $\theta$ and with it the count of crimes prevented. For car
prowls $\kappa$ itself stays between
`{python} f"{tab('carprowl', 'grid')['kappa'].min():.2f}"` and
`{python} f"{tab('carprowl', 'grid')['kappa'].max():.2f}"` across all
eight combinations, and crimes prevented between
`{python} num(tab('carprowl', 'grid')['prevented'].min())` and
`{python} num(tab('carprowl', 'grid')['prevented'].max())`.

# Discussion

The arrest term is a small change to a standard model, and it answers a
question the standard model cannot: of the crimes a crime would have
triggered, how many did the arrest stop? The estimate has a direct reading
for police. For car prowls in Seattle, an arrest at the scene all but ends
the elevated risk that follows a car prowl. A patrol response that catches
someone in the act is worth far more, for this purpose, than an arrest a
week later, because the risk the arrest can remove is gone within a day.

It also gives a sober accounting of scale. Near repeat patterns are
sometimes presented as if interrupting them would move crime totals. Here
the chains are short. If a car prowl triggers
`{python} f"{cp['theta']['exp']:.2f}"` others, then even arresting someone
at the scene of every car prowl would prevent, through this channel, fewer
than one in ten. The value of arrests for car prowls has to come mostly from
somewhere else, such as incapacitating people who offend at a high rate for
a long time or deterrence from the certainty of being caught [@nagin2013],
neither of which a triggering kernel measures. The shooting result says the
same thing more bluntly: with shootings in Chicago close to independent
given place and season, there is little chain in space and time to break.

Several limitations deserve mention. The estimate of $\kappa$ is
observational. Arrested crimes are not a random sample, and I have only
crude covariates to adjust for the difference; the simulation shows the
direction of the bias when a trait raises both productivity and the chance
of arrest. The arrest link is to one report, and an arrest that should be
credited against a string of an offender's crimes is credited against one.
Chicago's arrest table gives the case number for about 70% of arrests, so
some arrests for shootings are missing; the arrest shares match published
arrest rates closely but run a few points low for homicides, and a missing
arrest biases the estimate of $\kappa$ toward one. Both cities publish the
block and not the address, and Seattle's car prowl times are imprecise for
crimes discovered after the fact.
And the model's kernels are simple: one decay rate and one spatial scale for
everything, where sprees within a night and returns to the same place weeks
later are probably different processes.

Natural extensions follow from those. With offender identifiers, arrests
could dampen the kernels of all of a person's linked crimes at once. With
gang or group data, the retaliation channel for shootings could be modeled
on a network instead of in space [@green2017], where the question of whether
an arrest satisfies or provokes the other side has more bite. The same
dampening term would also work for any intervention attached to a crime
with a timestamp, such as a violence interrupter's response [@park2021] or a
victim services contact. The data requirement is the binding constraint.
Few cities publish which crime had an arrest and when, and of the large
cities I checked only Chicago does so for shootings completely enough to
use. Incident-based records reported to the FBI's National Incident-Based
Reporting System link arrests to offenses for thousands of agencies, but
without locations; a version of the model in time alone could use them,
and I plan to add that analysis.

# Appendix: sensitivity to the kernel and background {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-grid
#| tbl-cap: "Fits across temporal kernels and background smoothing ($k$ nearest neighbors; the median bandwidth is in meters). The row with the highest log-likelihood for each crime type is the one used in the paper."
rows = []
for c in CRIMES:
    g = tab(c, "grid")
    best = g["loglik"].idxmax()
    for i, r in g.iterrows():
        rows.append({
            "": CNAME[c] if i == 0 else "", "Kernel": {"exp": "Exponential", "lomax": "Power law"}[r["kernel"]],
            "k": int(r["k"]), "Bandwidth": num(r["median_bandwidth"]),
            "Log-likelihood": num(r["loglik"], 1) + (" *" if i == best else ""),
            "$\\theta$": f"{r['theta']:.3f}", "$\\kappa$": f"{r['kappa']:.2f}", "p ($\\kappa$ = 1)": pval(r["lr_p"]),
            "Median lag (days)": f"{r['median_days']:.2f}", "$\\sigma$": num(r["sigma"]),
            "Prevented": num(r["prevented"], 1),
        })
show(pd.DataFrame(rows), left=2)
```
